messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir is a 37-year-old firefighter who has been married for eleven years. He and his wife, Layla, live in a quiet suburban neighborhood where they had planned to start a family. That plan is now on hold. The change began eighteen months ago, after a medical call that seemed routine at the time—a man in his late twenties complaining of chest pain, agitated and alone in a cluttered apartment. Amir stayed with him until the ambulance arrived, speaking calmly, offering water. The man, whose name Amir later learned was Daniel, thanked him repeatedly. It did not seem unusual at the time.

Within a week, Daniel began appearing at the firehouse, asking for Amir by name. At first the others teased him about having a fan. Then Daniel started leaving notes on Amir’s car, sometimes just a single word: “Remember.” Amir told him to stop, formally, through the station captain. Daniel stopped coming to the station. Instead he began showing up in other places—outside the grocery store where Layla shopped, at the park where Amir ran on his days off. One afternoon, while Amir was cycling home on his bicycle, he heard tires on pavement too close behind him. He turned to see Daniel on a bicycle, matching his speed. Amir stopped and confronted him; Daniel just smiled and turned away. The police were called, a restraining order was filed, but Daniel never was located for service. He seemed to vanish. But the feeling of being watched, of being tracked, never vanished.

At first, Amir tried to explain it away as his own hypervigilance. He started taking different routes to work, avoiding the streets where Daniel had been seen. He stopped riding his bicycle entirely; he stored it in the basement and told himself he just didn’t have time. When he drove, he checked the rearview mirror obsessively. If a car followed him for more than two blocks, he would take a sudden detour, sometimes arriving late to a shift. He did not tell his colleagues why. The firehouse had always been a place of trust and camaraderie; he did not want them to see him as someone who could be unravelled by a single stalker.

At the scene of emergency calls, Amir became watchful in a different way. As soon as the engine stopped, he would scan the perimeter for exits, for places where someone could hide, for any face that did not belong. Unexpected sounds—a door slamming, a shout from bystanders, the clang of a dropped tool—made his heart pound and his vision narrow. He watched the people around him constantly, reading their hands, their eyes, their posture, searching for signs of threat. He knew he was doing it. He could not stop. Once, during a structure fire, he froze momentarily when a wall collapsed with a sound like a gunshot. The crew chief asked if he was okay; Amir said he was fine. He was not fine.

What frightened him most was what he could not control. Memories of the stalking could return without any warning—the smear of a bicycle tire on the pavement, the shape of a man’s silhouette in a window, even the smell of gasoline from the station’s pumps could drop him back into that moment of turning and seeing Daniel’s face, and the overwhelming terror would flood through him so completely that he had to stop whatever he was doing, sometimes holding onto a railing or a doorframe, unable to move until the wave passed. If anyone asked him what was wrong, he found he could not explain. The words would not come. He knew what had happened, but to describe it felt impossible, as though the memory existed in a part of his mind that had no language.

He had come to believe that he had been permanently damaged by the experience. He was certain that his reactions—the scanning, the startle, the avoidance—meant he was going crazy. And worse, he believed this proved he was a weak person. A firefighter was supposed to be steady under pressure. He could not even manage a single civilian’s obsession. In the quiet hours at the station, he would lie awake and think: *A strong man would have shaken this off. A strong man would not be undone by a bike ride.*

The breaking point came three weeks ago. Amir was dispatched to a car accident on a residential street. As he approached the scene, he saw a bicycle lying on the lawn near the wrecked vehicle. The sight stopped him. His mind went blank. He stood frozen at the curb while his crew worked, unable to take a step. His captain pulled him aside afterward and said, quietly, that he needed to get some help. Layla had been saying the same thing for months. That night, Amir called a number for a therapist who specialized in first responders. He is terrified that he will never feel like himself again, but he is even more terrified that he will lose his job, or his marriage, or both. He hopes, somewhere underneath the shame, that someone can show him how to live without watching every shadow.
